A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ICR research, with matching authors, method, and retained experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison. The original appendices A–C can be matched to v2 appendices B, C, and G.

before.justification: Version 1 reports original single-hop and multi-hop retrieval experiments, latency measurements, component ablations, and attention analyses in Sections 4–5 and the appendices.

after.justification: Version 2 retains these original results and adds TREC evaluations, document-order experiments, and ColBERTv2-based BEIR evaluations. The explicitly borrowed setwise results do not affect this assessment.

M1.justification: The prompts, attention aggregation, content-free calibration, token filtering, and document scoring remain unchanged. Although Figure 2's caption drops its mention of filtering, Section 3.3 and Equation (3) retain that operation.

E1.justification: Version 2 adds TREC-DL19 and TREC-DL20, extending single-hop evaluation to their MS MARCO passage-retrieval data. The nine BEIR datasets and three multi-hop datasets remain, making this a bounded expansion within the existing retrieval task.

E2.justification: Table F.4 adds RankVicuna and Setwise.heapsort/bubblesort with T5-XL on four BEIR datasets, substantially extending comparison beyond RankGPT to supervised and setwise approaches. The setwise scores are explicitly copied from Zhuang et al. (2024). Table E.3 also introduces ColBERTv2 as a single-hop retrieval baseline.

E3.justification: New evaluations compare retriever, reversed, and randomized document orders on TREC-COVID and MuSiQue, and use ColBERTv2 candidates for BEIR. These supplement the evaluation design; the original candidate counts, metrics, backbone models, RankGPT sliding window, and latency-test settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds a controlled test of sensitivity to document order. Appendix E examines whether benefits persist with a stronger first-stage retriever. Existing component ablations, candidate-count scaling, bias plots, and qualitative successes and failures are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix D newly reports means and standard deviations across five random seeds for shuffled document orders. Version 1 provides no corresponding repeated-seed uncertainty reporting. This practice is limited to the new experiment, with no stated increase in runs for retained results.

E6.justification: Substantial results are added in Table 1 and Appendices D–F. On the new DL19/DL20 tests, Llama-3.1 ICR scores 55.7/51.9 versus RankGPT's 64.9/63.9, exposing a performance weakness. ColBERTv2, ordering, and additional-baseline results further expand the evidence. Original BEIR per-dataset scores and Tables 2–4 remain unchanged; revised aggregates should not be interpreted as same-setting gains.

T1.justification: New Appendix A makes the sufficient-context assumption explicit and decomposes complexity into API calls, prefill passes, and decoding passes. It distinguishes O(1) listwise API calls from O(N) decoding passes. This refines the complexity argument; the method's equations remain unchanged and no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The central claims remain training-free attention-based reranking, two forward passes, guaranteed ranking outputs, competitive open-model performance, and reduced latency. Updated benchmark summaries do not redefine these contributions. The added abstract sentence restates the attention–relevance premise already present in v1 Section 3.2.

C2.justification: Version 2 asserts that attention normalization avoids length bias, speculates that MS MARCO-related fine-tuning explains Llama's TREC weakness, and connects ordering robustness to calibration and recency bias. Appendix F adds performance-versus-cost qualifications. The original lexical-bias and architectural limitations remain.

D1.justification: Version 2 specifies QA-style prompting for the new TREC datasets and identifies T5-XL and the borrowed-score provenance for setwise comparisons. Existing prompt templates, principal model checkpoints, KV caching, hardware, truncation details, and code/data access information are retained.

R1.justification: Craswell et al. (2020) is added for TREC. Discussion of the already-cited RankVicuna and setwise approaches expands to their training/inference costs and empirical relationship to ICR. The broader literature review and novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: There are targeted wording edits, an expanded abstract explanation, new appendix sections, and updated cross-references and publication headers. Existing prompts, limitations, and qualitative analyses are reorganized into appendices B, C, and G. The main narrative and most prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The quantitative presentation expands substantially: Table 1 gains two TREC columns, and new Tables A.1, D.2, E.3, and F.4 display complexity, ordering robustness, retriever comparisons, and additional baselines. Existing tables are resized or reformatted and appendix displays relocated. The original diagrams, plots, and qualitative evidence are retained.

improvement.justification: The added comparisons, ordering tests, and negative TREC results provide a limited net improvement in understanding ICR's applicability and weaknesses. Reporting errors constrain that benefit: Table 1 retains nine-dataset GPT macro-averages while updating open-model averages for eleven datasets, creating a misleading claimed macro-average win over GPT-3.5. Table D.2 also labels MuSiQue results Recall@5 while its retriever value, 37.9, matches Recall@2 in Table 2. The broader evidence is useful, but these inconsistencies prevent a major improvement.
